title: Pauri 37, sound: karam khandd

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saram Khand, the workshop. Your line was effort shapes the mind. Did you do one small thing with real care, start to finish? Today, the fourth realm, sound first. Day two hundred twenty-six.

Songwriters know a trick. You write a line, and later in the song you bring back its exact shape with one word changed, and the listener's ear lights up. The same frame, a new filling. It tells you: we've moved, but we're still in the same song. Yesterday's stanza gave us a frame: saram khandd kee baanee roop. The language of the realm of effort is beauty. Pauri 37 opens with that same frame, changes two words, and suddenly we're somewhere new. And one of the words it brings in is an old friend, the hammer from Pauri 33. Today, just listen for the echo.
screen: `THE SAME FRAME, A NEW WORD.` → `SARAM KHANDD KEE BAANEE ROOP.` → `LISTEN FOR THE ECHO.`

segments.voice: Here is the first line of Pauri 37: karam khandd kee baanee jor. Put it next to yesterday's: saram khandd kee baanee roop. Same frame. Saram becomes karam; roop becomes jor. Let's take the new words. Karam: grace, generosity, kindness freely given. It's a Persian word, and it's easy to confuse with karma, which means action and its results. Both appear in the Granth. Here, Sikh commentators generally read karam as grace. Karam khandd: the realm of grace. Kee baanee: its language, its mark. Jor: power, strength. The language of the realm of grace is power. Now remember Pauri 33, where jor hammered through every line with no beside it: no power to speak, no power to be silent, no power of our own. Here jor comes back, and there's no no. The power that wasn't ours is at home in the realm of grace. Then the second line: tithai hor na koee hor. Tithai: there. Hor: other, else. Na koee: not anyone. Hor again. There, no one else, no other at all. Hear how hor bookends the line, the way jor boxed in the lines of Pauri 33. The whole stanza has a strong, even beat; many hear it as the most majestic part of the Japji. Tomorrow we'll open who lives in this realm, and what lies beyond it. Today, listen to saram become karam, and jor come home.
screen: `SARAM BECOMES KARAM.` · `KARAM — GRACE, NOT KARMA.` · `JOR — POWER, AND NO NO THIS TIME.` · `TITHAI HOR NA KOEE HOR.` · then, large: `KARAM KHANDD.`

segments.voice: Say the first two lines aloud: karam khandd kee baanee jor, tithai hor na koee hor. Say them three times, with a strong, even beat. Then say yesterday's line once, saram khandd kee baanee roop, and today's once more, and hear the echo. Afterward, sit in silence. With each breath out, let yourself feel held by a strength that isn't yours to earn. Just rest in it. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 37. It opens in the realm of grace: karam khandd kee baanee jor, its language is power, and there is no one else, no other at all.
Your line: karam khandd, the realm of grace. Today, notice one good thing that came to you that you did nothing to earn. Day two hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 37 describes the last two of the five realms, and its opening, karam khandd kee baanee jor, echoes the frame of the line before it about Saram Khand.
